claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain than commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater fracture toughness than commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
The enhanced plastic strain and toughness are governed primarily by nanoscale Zr-rich precipitates.
The Zr-rich precipitates nucleate and grow both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Reducing the Zr content will reduce the formation of nanoscale Zr-rich precipitates.
Reducing the Zr content will lower plasticity relative to equimolar WTaTiVZr.
Reducing the Zr content will lower toughness relative to equimolar WTaTiVZr.
High-temperature lattice distortion induces compositional fluctuations that produce Zr-rich secondary phases.
Zr segregates and forms stable nanoscale precipitates during high-temperature exposure.
The Zr-rich precipitates impede dislocation motion.
The Zr-rich precipitates deflect propagating cracks.
Dislocation pinning by the precipitates enhances work hardening and plastic deformation.
Crack deflection by the precipitates enhances fracture toughness.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher yield strain than commercially pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr will undergo more plastic deformation before failure than commercially pure tungsten.
Commercially pure tungsten has a homogeneous high-temperature microstructure without significant nanoscale heterogeneity.
The proposed precipitation-controlled mechanism is valid from 900 to 1200 °C because this range permits sufficient atomic diffusion and precipitation kinetics.
At substantially lower temperatures or extreme deformation rates, mechanisms other than Zr-rich precipitation may dominate plasticity and toughness.
